question: Not shared at the level of population class. Both papers detect current (cross-sectional) MCI against non-MCI from clinical and questionnaire tabular data in Chinese hospital patients, so the task, comparison and channel match (the record's 'P-307 = retinal' is wrong; P-307 uses no imaging). The populations behind the label are two different disease-defined groups, and neither is a subset of the other. P-339 studies hospitalised type 2 diabetes patients aged 40-75 in an endocrinology department (Nanjing); P-307 studies patients aged 60 or over with chronic pain (IASP criteria) in a pain department (Nanchang; mean age 71.1). Each model is built on predictors tied to its population's defining condition: the Chinese visceral adiposity index in P-339; pain level, number of pain sites and pain duration (with depression and sleep scales) in P-307, where pain level is the top SHAP variable. The MCI definitions also differ: MoCA < 26 alone in P-339; Petersen/IWG criteria (memory complaint, MoCA < 26, ADL, MMSE-excluded dementia) with neurologist confirmation in P-307. P-307's authors treat MCI identification in chronic-pain patients as a question distinct from the one answered by existing models for diabetic patients.

figures.P-339: Logistic nomogram (age, gender, education, CVAI), 95% CIs as printed: training, apparent (n = 236; 109 MCI/127 NC) 0.765 [0.705, 0.826]; random 30% validation (n = 101; 49 MCI/52 NC) 0.690 [0.588, 0.792]; optimism-corrected C-index 0.747 [0.695, 0.800]. Hanley-McNeil check of the validation interval: Q1 = 0.5267, Q2 = 0.5634, SE = 0.0528, [0.587, 0.793], matching the printed one.
figures.P-307: Testing set (30%, n = 184; about 51 MCI/133 non-MCI at the cohort's 169/612 = 27.6%), 95% CIs as printed (Table 2): XGBoost 0.925 [0.863, 0.995]; LR 0.895 [0.829, 0.966]; SVM 0.757 [0.672, 0.844]. A Hanley-McNeil check for XGBoost at 51/133 gives Q1 = 0.8605, Q2 = 0.8890, SE = 0.0264, [0.873, 0.977]; the printed interval is wider and is used.

matched_figure_check: No figure is reported in the other's population or with the other's predictors, so nothing removes the population difference. On the matched validation stage (both internal random 70/30 splits), P-339's validation AUC 0.690 [0.588, 0.792] and P-307's test AUC 0.925 [0.863, 0.995] have non-overlapping intervals. On the same model class (logistic regression), P-339's nomogram 0.690 [0.588, 0.792] against P-307's LR 0.895 [0.829, 0.966] also does not overlap. The record's pairing (P-339's apparent training AUC 0.765 [0.705, 0.826] against 0.925) keeps the gap too. No matched figure reconciles the pair.
performance_validity: Section 3.5 exclusion not met: P-307's 0.925 is below 0.97 (n = 612, internal split only). A caution for any use of P-307's figure: its test-set precision (0.882) equals its specificity (0.882), which holds only at 1:1 class balance; at the test set's expected 27.6% prevalence the same sensitivity (0.885) and specificity would give precision of about 0.74 (45.1/(45.1 + 15.7)). The reported test metrics therefore appear to have been computed on class-balanced data, possibly after SMOTETomek resampling or within the 10-fold CV the methods mention, so 0.925 may be optimistic. P-339's figures are well below the ceiling.
reason: The AUCs differ beyond uncertainty at every matched validation stage and model class (0.690 [0.588, 0.792] against 0.925 [0.863, 0.995]), and no matched figure reconciles them. But they describe MCI detection in two different disease-defined populations (hospitalised adults with type 2 diabetes against older chronic-pain patients), with predictors specific to each condition and different MCI definitions, so the pair fails condition 1. P-307 does benchmark its AUC against a diabetes MCI model in its discussion, but it frames its own population as one that the diabetic models do not cover. If the operator read 'Chinese hospital patients screened with MoCA < 26' as one class, conditions 2 to 6 would hold, with population, predictors, MCI definition and P-307's apparently balanced evaluation as the candidate explanations.

quotes.quote: A total of 337 hospitalized patients with T2DM were included and randomly assigned to a training cohort (70%, n = 236) and a validation cohort (30%, n = 101).
MoCA score ≥ 26 is considered normal (NC group) and MoCA score <26 is considered MCI(MCI group)
identified four robust predictors in the training cohort: age, gender, education, and CVAI.
with AUC values of 0.765 (95% CI: 0.705–0.826) in the training cohort and 0.690 (95% CI 0.588–0.792) in the validation cohort (Fig. 4C, D).
A total of 612 older patients with chronic pain were recruited between October 2023 and July 2024.
Although many risk factors for MCI in older adults are worth considering [11], this needs further validation in this specific subgroup.
Although MCI prediction models have been developed for older patients with diabetes and chronic kidney disease, etc [12, 13]. , no such models exist for older patients with chronic pain.
The outcome of this study was the occurrence of MCI, which was diagnosed according to Petersen’s Criteria and the International Working Group on MCI
achieving a 1:1 balance between MCI-positive and non-MCI cases
To minimize random errors, all metrics were calculated using 10-fold cross validation.
We divided 428 samples (70%) into the training set, and 184 (30%) samples into the testing set.
the final selected variables were: age, education level, pain duration, number of pain sites, pain level, depression, sleep quality
the XGBoost model performed best, achieving an accuracy of 0.883 and an AUC of 0.925 (95% CI 0.863–0.995).
Jiang et al.'s traditional diabetes-based MCI prediction model reported an AUC of 0.893 [12]
